AboutPage.paragraphs:
My expertise with React and Next.js has allowed me to build dynamic and highly responsive user interfaces. I have developed complex single-page applications (SPAs) and server-side rendered (SSR) applications, ensuring optimal performance and user experience. Utilizing Typescript has enabled me to write robust and type-safe code, reducing bugs and enhancing maintainability. My deep understanding of Express has been crucial in developing scalable backend services and APIs, supporting the seamless integration of frontend and backend functionalities.
I have extensive experience in both creating and delivering projects from scratch and joining ongoing projects to refactor, rebuild, and ensure delivery with quality and performance. My proficiency in utilizing Scrum and agile methodologies ensures that projects are completed on time and to the highest standard. I place a strong emphasis on tracking all code with the best Git practices and tools.
As the founder, teacher, and mentor at Iniciativa Code!, a nonprofit organization, I guide individuals in technology for free. I have successfully assisted dozens of people in Brazil to start their tech careers through free courses, mentorship, and networking with tech companies.
My journey has also involved optimizing development processes and implementing best practices to enhance code quality and performance. By focusing on writing reusable and high-performing components, I ensure that applications are scalable and maintainable. My experience with modern CSS frameworks and libraries, such as Tailwind, SCSS, Styled-Components, ShadCN, ArkUI, PandaCss, ChakraUI, and Bootstrap, has allowed me to create visually appealing and user-friendly interfaces.
I am dedicated to continuously learning and growing in the field of software engineering, always aiming to deliver exceptional results and drive innovation.

JourneyPage.heroSubtitle: The experiences, principles, and values that continue shaping me as a software engineer, leader, and lifelong learner.
JourneyPage.principlesDescription: Three convictions sit underneath every decision I make — in the code I write and the way I try to work with people.
JourneyPage.principle1Description: My faith is the compass I return to when decisions are hard and answers aren't obvious. It keeps me humble, invites me to keep growing, and reminds me that technology is never the point — the people it serves always are.
JourneyPage.principle2Description: Software never stands still, and neither do I. Through curiosity, formal study, mentorship, and projects that stretch me, I try to end each day a slightly better engineer than I started it.
JourneyPage.principle3Description: Trust is the foundation of everything we build. Reliable software comes from acting honestly, respecting the people who use it, protecting their privacy, and choosing to build things that genuinely improve lives.
JourneyPage.timelineDescription: Every step built on the last — from a first curious line of code toward the engineer I'm still becoming.
JourneyPage.timeline1Description: My first lines of HTML and CSS turned a passing curiosity into a craft. Building things people could actually open and use was the moment I knew what I wanted to do.
JourneyPage.timeline2Description: Formal studies gave me the fundamentals — algorithms, data structures, and the discipline of writing code that others can read, trust, and maintain.
JourneyPage.timeline3Description: Where technical skill met purpose. I learned to pair engineering rigor with character, leadership, and a commitment to serve through the work I create.
JourneyPage.timeline4Description: My first taste of engineering at scale. Contributing to software used by millions taught me collaboration, code review, and the real weight of shipping to people.
JourneyPage.timeline5Description: Building production interfaces where design, performance, and reliability all matter at once — and where every decision has a real user on the other side.
JourneyPage.timeline6Description: Taking an idea from a blank file to a real product. Architecture, trade-offs, and ownership — learning what it truly means to carry something from zero to one.
JourneyPage.timeline7Description: To keep growing as an engineer and a leader — mentoring others, building technology that serves, and never losing the curiosity that started all of this.
JourneyPage.growthDescription: Each of these chapters stretched me technically — and, just as importantly, shaped the person doing the work.
JourneyPage.growth1Learned: How large engineering teams actually operate — reading unfamiliar code, writing tests, giving and receiving code reviews, and shipping changes safely into a system relied on by millions.
JourneyPage.growth1Professionally: I gained the confidence to contribute to a mature codebase and learned that clear communication and humility matter every bit as much as technical skill.
JourneyPage.growth1Personally: Working on software that helps families connect across generations reminded me that engineering can be profoundly meaningful — not just clever.
JourneyPage.growth2Learned: How to build and maintain production interfaces where performance, accessibility, and reliability are simply non-negotiable.
JourneyPage.growth2Professionally: I sharpened my ability to turn requirements into clean, maintainable components and to own features from first idea to production.
JourneyPage.growth2Personally: I learned patience and care for detail — that small, deliberate improvements compound into products people genuinely enjoy using.
JourneyPage.growth3Learned: What it takes to design a product from scratch — the architecture decisions, the trade-offs, and the quiet discipline of actually finishing.
JourneyPage.growth3Professionally: I grew into a more complete engineer: product thinking, prioritization, and the courage to make good decisions with incomplete information.
JourneyPage.growth3Personally: Building something of my own taught me resilience — that real progress comes from showing up consistently, especially when it's hard.
JourneyPage.valuesHeading: Software engineering is more than writing code
JourneyPage.valuesParagraph1: The syntax is the easy part. The work that actually matters lives in the space around the code — how we treat the people we build with, the honesty we bring to hard trade-offs, and the care we take with the humans on the other side of the screen.
JourneyPage.valuesParagraph2: Ethics, teamwork, communication, leadership, empathy, ownership, and a habit of continuous improvement aren't “soft” skills to me. They are the foundation that lets good engineering hold up under real-world weight.
JourneyPage.quoteText: Technology has the greatest impact when it is built with competence, integrity, and a genuine desire to serve others.
JourneyPage.quoteByline: A principle I try to build by
JourneyPage.ethicsDescription: Studying where others went wrong is one of the clearest ways to decide the kind of engineer you want to be.
JourneyPage.ethicsCaseSummary: A story less about a technical failure and more about the choices a company makes after one — and what those choices teach the rest of us about integrity in software.
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock1Title: A breach — and then a cover-up
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock1Body: In 2016, attackers reached the personal data of roughly 57 million Uber riders and drivers after finding cloud credentials that had been left in a private code repository. Rather than disclosing it, Uber paid the attackers $100,000 to quietly delete the data and stayed silent for about a year, disguising the payment as a routine bug bounty.
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock2Title: The concealment, not just the mistake
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock2Body: Breaches can happen to anyone; hiding one is a choice. Concealing it stripped millions of people of the chance to protect themselves, treated a security failure as a PR problem, and broke the basic trust users place in the software they rely on. It ultimately led to a $148 million settlement and a criminal conviction for the executive who orchestrated the cover-up.
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock3Title: Transparency is part of the engineering
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock3Body: Secrets don't belong in source control, security has to be designed in rather than bolted on, and honesty is not optional when something goes wrong. How an organization responds to a breach reveals its real values far more clearly than its mission statement ever could.
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock4Title: The engineer I want to be
JourneyPage.ethicsBlock4Body: If I'm ever close to a situation like this, I want to be the person who says the hard thing early — who reports the issue, protects the users first, and helps the team do the right thing even when it's costly. Competence keeps systems safe; character keeps them honest.
JourneyPage.reflectionParagraph1: Ensign College taught me that growth is never only technical. Alongside the engineering, I learned to lead, to communicate clearly, and to tie my work to something bigger than a passing grade — a habit I hope to keep for the rest of my career.
JourneyPage.reflectionParagraph2: My internships turned theory into confidence. Shipping real features, alongside experienced engineers, into systems people actually depend on showed me that I belong in this work — and that I still have so much room to grow.
JourneyPage.reflectionParagraph3: So I intend to keep learning, on purpose and for good. New languages, better patterns, harder problems, and the wisdom of people further down the road than I am — curiosity is the one skill I never want to outgrow.
JourneyPage.reflectionParagraph4: Most of all, I want the technology I build to leave people better off: a little more connected, a little more capable, a little more trusting of the tools in their hands. That, to me, is what makes this career worth doing.
JourneyPage.reflectionQuoteStart: I believe the best software engineers never stop learning, never stop serving, and never stop
JourneyPage.referencesDescription: A few sources that have quietly shaped the way I think about work, character, and the responsibility that comes with building things for other people.
JourneyPage.reference1Detail: On choosing to act with initiative and to do good of one's own free will — a reminder that ownership and agency shape everything we build.
JourneyPage.reference2Detail: On trust and humility when the path forward isn't clear — a principle I lean on when engineering decisions carry real weight.
JourneyPage.reference3Detail: Talks on integrity, service, and lifelong learning that quietly shaped how I try to show up in my work and with the people around me.
